title: Ang 1389–1398: the Bhatts on the first Gurus
hook: the court poets praise Nanak, Angad and Amar Das
tomorrow: one name for God rings out over and over in their praise. which?

segments.voice: Yesterday, on ang 1385, Guru Arjan's swayyas: praise, whether it turns the singer or says love out loud. Now the praise turns to the Gurus.

At a wedding, a cousin grabs the mic and the room changes: the voice gets bigger, the rhythm starts rolling, everyone leans in. The Bhatts were poets like that, bards whose craft was praise, sung aloud. On ang 1389 their swayyas begin, and they turn their praise on the Gurus, starting with Guru Nanak. So what did these poets hear in the Gurus?
screen: `SOMEONE GRABS THE MIC.` → `THE BHATTS: PRAISE, SUNG ALOUD.` → `WHAT DID THEY HEAR?`

segments.voice: Start with the sound. A Bhatt's swayya is built to be sung loud, line after line landing on a strong beat, names repeated like a drum. The first set, headed for the first Guru, sings Guru Nanak, and in paraphrase it lists who sings his praises: the sky and the earth, sages and yogis, the figures of the old stories, as if the whole world had joined the chorus. Then Guru Angad. The Bhatts call him Lehna, the name he had before, and sing of the light that was in Nanak now shining in him. Then Guru Amar Das, praised as the same light again. Listen for what the beat keeps hammering. Not three famous men, one after another, but one light in a new body each time. That's what the Bhatts hear. And the beat is part of the teaching. A sentence can tell you the light passed on. A swayya makes you feel it land, line, line, line.
screen: `BUILT TO BE SUNG LOUD.` · `THE WHOLE WORLD SINGS NANAK.` · `LEHNA BECOMES ANGAD.` · `ONE LIGHT, A NEW BODY EACH TIME.` · then, large: `PRAISE OF THE GURUS.`

segments.voice: Tap a slow, steady beat on your knee, once with each breath out. After a little while stop tapping, and keep hearing the beat inside through the sit. That's the shape of a swayya: you keep hearing it after it ends.
Ang 1389. Where the Bhatts' swayyas begin, praising Guru Nanak, then Guru Angad and Guru Amar Das, as one light.
To keep: praise of the gurus, one light, sung loud enough to feel in your chest. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: The Bhatts' swayyas are read in the closing pages of the Granth and sung in kirtan, especially on the Gurus' gurpurabs, the days that remember them.

fork.setup: your dad asks why the gurdwara sings praise of the Gurus, not only of God. what do the Bhatts' swayyas give you?
options: they praise the same light in each Guru, the One's light, passing on.
they show the Gurus wanted to be worshiped as gods in their own right.
they were court flattery, kept only because the poets were famous.
fork.reveal: the Bhatts hear one light, in Nanak, in Lehna who became Angad, in Amar Das. the praise is for that light.

original.note: Gurmukhi: Bhatt, a bard; the Bhatts' swayyas begin on ang 1389.

what a scholar hears: the swayyas are headed by the Guru they praise, and Guru Angad appears under his earlier name, Lehna.

chat.says: writing a thank you to my old gurmukhi teacher for my rec letter. 'thanks for everything' feels flat
options: do what the Bhatts did: name her, and name the light you saw in her, line by line.
keep it vague; the Bhatts praised the Gurus in big, general words, never names.
skip the praise; the Bhatts teach that praising a person takes away from God.
chat.meaning: The Bhatts praise each Guru by name, in a ringing beat, and hear the same light in each. Praise that names lands.

Bhatts.meaning: bards whose craft was praise; their swayyas are in the Granth

Lehna.meaning: Guru Angad's name before he became the second Guru
